def Target : Prop :=
  ∀ (P D E R : Type) (t : S3 P D E R), t.D23 →

      (∃ p, ∃ o ∈ t.c1 p, w p ∉ t.c2 o)

translation:
Target defines (without asserting or proving) the following proposition.

For all types P, D, E, and R (with no finiteness, nonemptiness, or other restrictions) and every structure t of type S3 P D E R—consisting of a function c1 assigning a subset of D to each element of P, a function c2 assigning a subset of E to each element of D, a function c3 from D to R, and a function c4 from R to E—suppose t satisfies the following hypothesis (t.D23):

- For every r in R, if there exists o in D such that c3 o = r and o belongs to c1 p0 for some p0 in P (that is, o is in the union t.D17 of all sets c1 p0), then there exist a function S from the set A(r) = {p in P | there exists o in c1 p with c3 o = r} (t.D19 r) to itself and an element p in A(r) such that the union U(p) = {e in E | there exists o in c1 p with e in c2 o} (t.D20 p) and the union U(S p) are disjoint (U(p) ∩ U(S p) = ∅). Note that S is only required to satisfy this disjointness condition at the single existentially chosen element p, not for all elements of A(r), and S p is not required to be distinct from p (so the condition is equivalent to the existence of two not necessarily distinct elements p, q in A(r) with U(p) ∩ U(q) = ∅).

Then, for every function w from P to E, at least one of the following two conditions holds (which disjunct holds may depend on P, D, E, R, t, and w):

1. For every r in R for which there exist p0 in P and o0 in c1 p0 with c3 o0 = r, there exist p in P and o in c1 p (which may depend on r) such that c3 o = r and c4 r ≠ w p.
2. There exist p in P and o in c1 p such that w p is not in c2 o.

Note what is not required: the hypothesis places no constraint on c4 (which appears only in disjunct 1); disjunct 1 requires only that some p and o in c1 p with c3 o = r satisfy c4 r ≠ w p, not all such p and o; and disjunct 2 requires only a single o in c1 p with w p ∉ c2 o, rather than w p ∉ c2 o for every o in c1 p. None of the other context definitions (such as S1, S2, or D18) appear in Target.

divergences.description: Disjunct 1 materially weakens the source claim. The passage states that unless the theory is already falsified, 'every single inference operation is wrong' and 'no single inference inf(or) points at the correct experience, so that the inference procedure is completely wrong' (contrasted with 'at least one of the inferred experiences inf(or) is correct'). Target only states `∀ r, t.D22 r → ∃ p, ∃ o ∈ t.c1 p, t.c3 o = r ∧ t.c4 r ≠ w p`: for each arising inference content `r`, there exists at least one system and dataset producing `r` where `inf(r)` disagrees with the true experience `w p`. Under Target, every prediction can be correct while `inf(r)` still equals `w p` (points at the true experience) on other systems producing `r`—even on all non-substituted systems for every `r`—so Target only establishes that no inference rule `r ↦ inf(r)` is universally valid across all systems producing `r`, rather than that every inference application is wrong or that no inference points at the true experience (the stronger universal reading is in fact false under `w : P → E`).

The paper's formalism has no formal 'true experience', and Target introduces `w : P → E` attached to the physical system rather than to datasets `D` or pairs `P × D` (declared by the author). This idealization assumes each physical system has a single true experience across all datasets `o ∈ t.c1 p` it can produce, which weakens the universal quantification over `w` compared to `w : P × D → E` (for example, any system admitting two datasets with disjoint predictions trivially satisfies Disjunct 2 for every `w : P → E`, without using `t.D23`).

Disjunct 2 (`∃ p, ∃ o ∈ t.c1 p, w p ∉ t.c2 o`) formalizes 'the theory under consideration is already falsified' as semantic falsity of some prediction, omitting any link to a formal falsification instance `t.D18 o` (`t.c4 (t.c3 o) ∉ t.c2 o`) or to an inference being correct at that dataset (`t.c4 (t.c3 o) = w p`), whereas the passage ties falsification to a correct inferred experience whose corresponding prediction is wrong.

judgement.summary: Target diverges materially from Proposition 3.7 and its accompanying explanation by weakening 'every single inference operation is wrong' / 'no single inference inf(or) points at the correct experience' to an existential counterexample per arising inference content `r`, allowing `inf(r)` to still identify the true experience on other systems producing `r` even when all predictions are accurate. It also makes the declared modeling choice of attaching a single true experience `w : P → E` to each physical system and formalizes 'already falsified' simply as some prediction excluding `w p` without linking it to `t.D18`.
